exercises.prompt:
What does this program print? Write the three lines separated by single spaces.

```scala
case class Book(title: String, year: Int)

@main def ex(): Unit =
  val a = Book("Ficciones", 1944)
  val b = a.copy(year = 1956)
  println(a == Book("Ficciones", 1944))
  println(b.year - a.year)
  println(a)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. `copy` returns a new book; `a` itself still has the year 1944.

hints: Case classes compare by their fields.
`copy` builds a new instance and leaves the original alone.
A case class's `toString` is its name followed by its fields, separated by commas with no spaces.
exercises.solution: `a` equals a freshly built `Book("Ficciones", 1944)` because case classes have structural equality: `true`. `b` is a copy with year 1956, so `b.year - a.year` is `12`. `a` is unchanged and prints as `Book(Ficciones,1944)`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print? Write the two values separated by a space.

```scala
class A(val n: Int)
case class B(n: Int)

@main def ex(): Unit =
  println(A(1) == A(1))
  println(B(1) == B(1))
```
hints: How does an ordinary class decide equality, unless you override `equals`?
exercises.solution: An ordinary class inherits `equals` from `AnyRef`, which compares identity: two separate `A` objects are different, so `false`. A case class gets structural equality, comparing fields: `true`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print? Write the three lines separated by single spaces.

```scala
def classify(xs: List[Int]): String = xs match
  case Nil                  => "empty"
  case x :: Nil             => s"one: $x"
  case x :: y :: _ if x > y => "starts by falling"
  case _ :: rest            => s"then ${rest.length} more"

@main def ex(): Unit =
  println(classify(List(5, 3, 8)))
  println(classify(List(1, 3, 8)))
  println(classify(List(9)))
```
answers: starts by falling then 2 more one: 9
hints: Cases are tried from top to bottom.
`x :: y :: _` matches lists with at least two elements; the guard then compares the first two.
`x :: Nil` matches a list with exactly one element.
exercises.solution: `List(5, 3, 8)`: not empty, not a single element, and 5 > 3, so `starts by falling`. `List(1, 3, 8)`: the guard fails (1 is not greater than 3), so the last case matches, with `rest` = `List(3, 8)`: `then 2 more`. `List(9)` matches `x :: Nil`: `one: 9`.

exercises.prompt:
What does this print?

```scala
val limit = 10
val r = 3 match
  case limit => s"matched $limit"
println(r)
```

options.label: `matched 3`
options.feedback: Yes. A lowercase name in a pattern introduces a new variable that matches anything; it shadows the outer `limit`.

options.label: `matched 10`
options.feedback: Not yet. The pattern does not refer to the outer `limit`; it binds a new `limit` to the value being matched, which is 3.

options.label: It throws a `MatchError`, because 3 is not 10.
options.feedback: Not yet. That would happen with `` case `limit` => `` (backticks compare against the existing value), not with a plain lowercase name.

options.label: It does not compile.
options.feedback: Not yet. It compiles; a variable pattern is legal, it just does not do what the author probably intended.

hints: In a pattern, what does a name starting with a lowercase letter mean?
exercises.solution: The pattern `limit` is a variable pattern: it matches any value and binds it to a *new* name `limit`, hiding the outer one. So it matches 3 and the result is `matched 3`. To compare with the existing value, write `` case `limit` => `` or `case n if n == limit =>`.

exercises.prompt: `enum Light: case Red, Amber, Green`. Which `match` makes the compiler warn that it may not be exhaustive?

options.label: `l match { case Light.Red => 1; case Light.Green => 3 }`
options.feedback: Yes. `Amber` is not handled, and the compiler names it in the warning.

options.label: `l match { case Light.Red => 1; case _ => 0 }`
options.feedback: Not yet. The wildcard handles every remaining case, so the match is exhaustive (though it will not warn you if a new case is added later).

options.label: `l match { case Light.Red | Light.Amber => 1; case Light.Green => 3 }`
options.feedback: Not yet. The alternative pattern covers Red and Amber, and Green has its own case: all three are handled.

options.label: None of them; Scala never checks exhaustiveness for enums.
options.feedback: Not yet. Checking exhaustiveness is one of the main benefits of enums and sealed traits.

hints: List the cases each match handles.
exercises.solution: Only (a) leaves a case unhandled (`Amber`). The compiler reports `match may not be exhaustive. It would fail on pattern case: Amber`. Note the trade-off in (b): a wildcard silences the check forever, so if a case is added later the compiler cannot point you to this match. Prefer listing the cases explicitly.

exercises.prompt: Which of these does the compiler generate for `case class Point(x: Double, y: Double)`? Choose all that apply.

options.label: `equals` and `hashCode` based on `x` and `y`
options.feedback: Yes. That is what makes two points with the same coordinates equal and usable as Set elements or Map keys.

options.label: A `copy` method with a parameter per field
Setter methods `x_=` and `y_=` to change the fields
options.feedback: Not yet. Case class fields are `val`s, so there are no setters. You make changed copies instead.

options.label: An extractor so that `case Point(a, b) =>` works in a match
options.feedback: Yes. Constructor patterns on case classes come for free.

options.label: A `toString` such as `Point(3.0,4.0)`
options.feedback: Yes, and it is very handy when debugging.

hints: Case classes are for immutable data.
exercises.solution: A case class gets structural `equals`/`hashCode`, `toString`, `copy`, a companion `apply` (so no `new` is needed) and an extractor (`unapply`) for patterns. Its fields are immutable `val`s, so no setters are generated.
